Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For a civilian assault trauma, 'talks about military' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the assault specifically involved military context, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It is not supported by the other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' implies a trauma involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty context. That does not cohere with the rest of this profile, which otherwise describes an individual assault without any indication that others were killed.

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: This appraisal is the main incoherent item in the profile. The rest of the report is organized around fear, betrayal, hypervigilance, male-related/interpersonal triggers, and fragmented sensory trauma memory after assault. In contrast, fearing that she will lose control of her own rage and do something terrible introduces a perpetration/anger-control theme that is not supported by the triggers, threat items, or memory content. It does not fit the dominant cognitive formulation in which negative appraisals feed threat and memory; the other appraisal items plausibly amplify fear and mistrust, but this one points to a different clinical concern not otherwise represented in the profile. Given the otherwise tightly fear-based assault presentation, this item is hard to integrate clinically with the selected set.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: This threat item is the least coherent element in the profile. The rest of the selected triggers, appraisals, and memory items consistently describe an interpersonal assault formulation centered on men, betrayal, mistrust, conversational/emotional triggers, and trauma memories. By contrast, needing to stay alert at night implies a more generalized ongoing danger-monitoring pattern that is not specifically supported by the selected triggers or appraisals. It is not impossible in PTSD, but here it fits less well than the other threat items and is weakly linked to the formulation, especially because Threat has no active edge to Maladaptive Strategies and the profile lacks other nighttime/sleep-related material.

vignette:
Marguerite is a fifty-four-year-old married woman who works as a chef in a busy restaurant kitchen. She came to therapy at the urging of her husband, who had grown increasingly worried about the changes he had seen in her over the past eight months. She is thin and tense, her hands folded tightly in her lap as she speaks, her eyes scanning the room even in the relative safety of the office.

The event that changed everything happened on a Tuesday evening in late autumn. Marguerite had stayed late after service to do inventory, and the kitchen was quiet except for the hum of the walk-in cooler. A new prep cook, a man in his late twenties who had been hired three weeks earlier, had lingered behind. She had thought nothing of it at first—he had seemed reliable, even friendly. But when she turned from the dry storage shelves, he was standing much closer than she had expected. He backed her against the steel counter, his hand on her shoulder, his voice low and insistent. She froze. He did not strike her, but he did not stop when she asked him to. He spoke to her in a way that made her feel small and trapped, his body blocking the door. It lasted only a few minutes before a dishwasher returning for a forgotten jacket startled them both, and the man stepped back and walked out. Marguerite told no one. She finished the inventory, locked up, and drove home.

In the weeks that followed, Marguerite found that she could not describe what had happened. When her husband asked why she seemed distant, she said she was tired. When a friend asked if something was wrong, she said it was nothing. The truth was that the event would not come to her in words. Instead, it came in flashes—the cold metal of the counter against her lower back, the smell of garlic and sweat, the weight of a hand on her shoulder. These pieces arrived without context, disconnected from one another, so that sometimes she would be standing at the stove and suddenly feel herself pinned again, her body rigid, her breath shallow, as if she were still pressed against that counter. She could not tell the story because there was no story—only fragments that did not fit together.

At work, Marguerite began to notice changes in how she moved through the kitchen. She had always been a commanding presence, calling out orders and tasting sauces with her fingers. Now she flinched whenever someone came up behind her. A busboy reaching past her for a plate would make her jerk sideways. She began to avoid the walk-in cooler altogether, sending junior staff to fetch what she needed. She found herself scanning the dining room during service, watching the door, checking the faces of men she did not know. When a stranger approached the pass to ask a question, her heart would pound before she even heard what he was saying.

She stopped staying late. She stopped training new hires if they were male. She began to feel that the world was full of people who could hurt her and that she could never know which ones would. The man had seemed kind. He had smiled. He had asked about her grandchildren. And then he had cornered her. She had trusted him because he worked for her, because she had trained him, because he had seemed ordinary. Now she believed that trust itself was a trap. She began to watch her husband differently. When he came up behind her in the kitchen at home, she would startle. When he tried to hold her at night, she would lie still, her body tense, waiting for something she could not name. She did not tell him why. She could not find the words.

The consequences accumulated slowly. She stopped attending the monthly dinner parties she and her husband had hosted for decades. She stopped walking their dog in the evening. She began to drink a glass of wine before bed, then two, to quiet the watchfulness that kept her awake. Her husband grew hurt and then frustrated. He accused her of pulling away. She said nothing. At work, her sous chef noticed that she had stopped going into the walk-in and that she flinched whenever the new line cook walked past. Marguerite told him she was fine. She was not fine.

What finally brought her to seek help was a morning in the kitchen at home, when her husband walked up behind her to kiss her neck, a gesture he had made a thousand times, and she spun around with a chef’s knife in her hand. She saw the shock on his face. She saw the fear. She put the knife down and began to cry. She came to therapy because she could not keep living like this, and because she was terrified that she would never feel safe again, and because she could not bear the thought that the man who had cornered her had taken not just that evening, but her marriage, her kitchen, her life.
